directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; kisoana primrose spreads readily by rhizome to form a colorful groundcover, unlike most primrose species that stay in a tight clump. Primula kisoana is a Japanese woodland species with soft, velvety, rounded leaves and clusters of bright rose-pink to magenta flowers held just above the foliage in mid-spring, spreading by underground rhizomes to form an expanding patch rather than remaining a single clump like most primroses. Its spreading habit makes it a useful flowering groundcover for a shaded woodland garden, filling in around hosta, fern, and Solomon's seal within a few seasons once established. It appreciates consistent moisture through the growing season and a winter mulch of leaf litter, and can be divided in fall to control spread or propagate new plantings.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before setting out and transplant in cool weather into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; wear gloves when handling German primrose, since the leaf hairs contain primin, a compound that causes contact dermatitis in some people.

Primula obconica is a Chinese species long grown as a cool-season flowering pot and bedding plant, with soft, rounded, hairy leaves and clusters of round-faced flowers in white, pink, red, salmon, and purple held above the foliage over a long cool-weather bloom period. It is grown as a winter or early-spring bedding and container plant in mild climates or as a greenhouse and indoor flowering plant further north, valued for its long bloom season and wide color range in shaded or filtered-light conditions. Because sensitive individuals can develop a skin rash from contact with the glandular hairs, primin-free modern cultivars are available and preferable for households with skin sensitivities or young children.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's saxifrage blooms in autumn rather than spring, unlike most saxifrage species, providing late-season color in a shaded border.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's saxifrage blooms in autumn rather than spring, unlike most saxifrage species, providing late-season color in a shaded border. Saxifraga fortunei is an East Asian woodland species with glossy, rounded, sometimes bronze-tinted leaves forming a neat mound, sending up airy, branched sprays of small, asymmetrical white flowers with elongated lower petals in autumn, often continuing until the first hard frost. Its distinctive fall bloom time sets it apart from spring-flowering saxifrages and makes it a valuable late-season companion for toad lily and fall-blooming anemone in a shaded border. Give it consistent moisture and protection from harsh winter wind, and mulch lightly in colder parts of its range to protect the crown over winter.

Astilbe rivularis is an imposing Himalayan and Chinese species dwarfing the familiar garden astilbe hybrids, with large, coarsely divided leaves and towering, airy, branched plumes of tiny greenish-white to pale pink flowers in summer that can reach shoulder height in ideal conditions. Its massive scale makes it a dramatic architectural specimen for a boggy, shaded streamside planting or the back of a large woodland border, standing out among smaller-scale shade perennials. It demands considerably more moisture than typical astilbe cultivars, thriving at a pond edge or in a rain garden where its roots never dry out, and struggles in drier garden conditions that ordinary astilbe would tolerate.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Henry's rodgersia has more finely cut, coppery-tinted foliage than other rodgersia species and benefits from a sheltered site out of drying wind.

Rodgersia henrici is a Chinese woodland species with deeply divided, palmately compound leaves emerging bronze-copper in spring before maturing to dark green, and airy, branched plumes of small creamy-white to pale pink, astilbe-like flowers held well above the foliage in summer. Its finely textured, coppery new growth distinguishes it from the coarser-leaved rodgersia species more commonly grown, adding another layer of foliage interest to a shaded bog garden or streamside planting. Give it constant moisture and rich soil, and protect the large, thin leaves from wind, which can tatter the foliage and dull its bronze coloring.
